component.name: Rehome
component.summary: Turn installed operating systems into virtual machines

description.p: Rehome gives an installed operating system a new home as a QEMU/KVM virtual machine. Point it at a physical disk or a disk image and it identifies the system, applies the fixes it needs to boot on virtual hardware, and starts it — without ever writing to the original disk.
It also creates and manages virtual machines from scratch:

ul.li: Imports Windows (from DOS and Windows 95 to Windows 11 and Server 2025), Linux and the BSDs
Supports physical disks, raw, E01, VHD/VHDX, VMDK, VDI and qcow2 images
Embedded console with clipboard sharing, dynamic resolution and USB redirection
Appliances: a drive image that boots a computer straight into a VM, full screen
Follows your desktop's light/dark style and accent colour

description.p: Windows 95/98/ME: the VGA BIOS no longer uses a stack of its own in upper memory, which Windows maps for each of its virtual machines. Windows 98 hung at a black screen with a blinking cursor when it shut down.

Appliances: a laptop's touchpad drives DOS and Windows 9x VMs directly, with tap to click and two-finger scrolling, instead of stopping at the screen's edges. Diagnostics of a running VM include the BIOS's video state, the code the processor runs and its stack.
Windows 95/98/ME: the VM turns off a few seconds after Windows has finished shutting down ("It's now safe to turn off your computer"), also without the APM driver in Windows.
Windows 95/98/ME: text before Windows starts is shown correctly again (0.3.16 dropped every other character with KVM), and Windows 98 no longer hangs at a black screen when it shuts down.
Windows 95/98/ME: the VGA BIOS no longer keeps its stack in upper memory, which Windows uses for other things, so Windows 98 no longer hangs at a black screen when it shuts down.
Diagnostics of a running VM say where its processor is (its mode, the code it runs, whether it is halted), to find out where a guest hangs.

Windows 95/98/ME VMs get a VGA BIOS without debug output, so Windows 98 no longer stops with "A fatal exception 0D has occurred at C000:00002007" when it shuts down. The appliance's maintenance console shows an error instead of closing when one of its pages fails.
Appliances: the VM starts again after a backup was restored or the maintenance password was changed in the maintenance console.

Appliances: the start screen no longer mentions the maintenance console (M still opens it), and the console can back the VM up to a USB drive and restore it, put CD/DVD images from a USB drive in, change memory, date and time, sound, screen and the password, choose what happens at power-on and when the VM shuts down, and show storage and logs.
Appliances of DOS and Windows 9x VMs: the computer's mice go straight to the VM's PS/2 mouse, so the pointer no longer stops at invisible edges.
Windows 95 and 98 no longer stop with "While initializing device NDIS: Windows protection error" on fast computers: Rehome applies patcher9x's fix to NDIS.VXD and the disk drivers in the VM's disk.

The mouse moves again in DOS and Windows 9x VMs: the console took their PS/2 mouse for an absolute one. Once captured, the guest cursor jumps to where you clicked, follows the pointer without Windows' acceleration getting in the way, and lines up again at every screen edge.

Switching a Windows VM to the faster virtio devices no longer leaves Windows unable to start: Rehome first makes the virtio disk driver load at boot, and keeps devices Windows has no driver for. Reverting to the checkpoint taken before the switch also restores the previous devices.

Windows 95 and 98 disks prepared on Linux start: Rehome writes its own boot sector, which starts IO.SYS the way grub4dos does, instead of SYSLINUX, which stopped at "Booting...". Rehome also warns when a Windows 9x partition reaches past 128 GiB.
DOS and Windows 9x boot repair also works when libguestfs's helper has no SYSLINUX: Rehome then uses this computer's own syslinux.
DOS and Windows 9x disks whose boot sector was written on Linux are made bootable even when libguestfs lacks mtools; failed automatic fixes show their technical details.
Appliances no longer report a normal shutdown or restart of the VM as a crash.
Windows XP chosen by hand in the New VM wizard gets the XP guest tools instead of virtio-win, which no longer supports it; Windows 7 gets the guest tools libosinfo lists for it.

Appliances keep Windows VMs' clocks right (the build computer's time zone, internet time); Windows XP can use resolutions up to 2560×1600 with the SPICE guest tools and QXL graphics; the screen no longer shows "Starting" while the computer turns off.

Appliances: the VM gets network through the computer's Wi-Fi even when it starts before the Wi-Fi is connected; a laptop's built-in camera, fingerprint reader and Bluetooth stay with the appliance (giving them to Windows XP VMs could crash them); when the VM stops unexpectedly, the maintenance console says why.

Choose where disk images are stored, for example on a second drive. Replace a VM's disk with another image or a new empty disk. Installer ISOs that libosinfo does not know (new releases, derivatives such as Omarchy) are recognised from their files, and the detected system can be changed in the New VM wizard.
Appliances: the VM fills the screen and the pointer reaches all of it; modern guests get the screen's native resolution.
Appliances: turn a VM into a drive image that boots a computer straight into it, full screen, with a hidden maintenance console.
